questions.question: Explain why France occupied the Ruhr in January 1923. (4 marks)
questions.correctAnswer: France occupied the Ruhr because Germany defaulted on reparations payments - specifically failing to deliver timber (December 1922) and coal (January 1923). French Prime Minister Poincaré was determined to enforce the Treaty of Versailles and believed taking resources directly was the only way to ensure payment.

questions.question: How far did hyperinflation affect all groups in German society equally? (8 marks)
questions.correctAnswer: Hyperinflation did NOT affect all groups equally. Borrowers benefited because they could repay debts with worthless money. Industrialists who sold goods for foreign currency profited. Farmers benefited because food retained real value. questions.correctAnswer: The government pursued passive resistance to show Germany would not accept French demands passively, to maintain national dignity, and because it could not afford to pay reparations. questions.question: Full-Mark Response 8 marks: Explain the effects of hyperinflation in 1923. <div class="
questions.correctAnswer: Hyperinflation devastated savers and those on fixed incomes. By November 1923, 4.2 trillion marks equalled $1 USD. A loaf of bread that cost 1 mark in 1919 cost 200,000 million marks by November 1923. Pensioners' fixed incomes became worthless overnight; a university professor's salary of 24,000 marks per year would not buy a newspaper. Some people resorted to burning banknotes as fuel because they were cheaper than coal. The middle class — Germany's natural defenders of democracy — never fully trusted the Republic again, associating democratic government with economic chaos. However, borrowers benefited enormously. Loans could be repaid with worthless money — a mortgage of 100,000 marks could be paid off with a few eggs' worth of cash. Industrialists like Hugo Stinnes who sold goods for stable foreign currency grew rich. Farmers benefited because food retained real value. The psychological impact was profound: the experience created a culture of "never again," but different groups drew opposite conclusions — some supported democracy, others turned to extremism, fueling the Munich Putsch (November 1923) and the Hamburg Communist Uprising (October 1923). Recovery came under Stresemann, who ended passive resistance in September 1923 and introduced the Rentenmark in November 1923, backed by land and industrial assets at a rate of 1 Rentenmark = 1 trillion old marks.
